source.title: The Non-Linear Representation Dilemma: Is Causal Abstraction Enough for Mechanistic Interpretability?
source.authors: De Sutter; Julian Minder; Thomas Hofmann; Tiago Pimentel

page_placements.theme: Alignment success requires capacity and generalization controls

record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates IOI algorithm alignments with DAS and argues that high interchange-intervention accuracy can occur even in randomly initialized models, challenging what causal-abstraction results establish about a mechanism. It does not test the GPT-2 small head circuit itself.
record.gate_note: The IOI experiments apply DAS interchange interventions to Pythia models using the ABAB-ABBA algorithm, not the 26-head GPT-2 small circuit. They do not ablate or patch the named head classes or test their roles. Exact IIA values in the relevant figures are not stated in the text; the rows record the authors’ textual descriptions. The study also reports results for the training/evaluation split with distinct names, which are recorded below.
record.test_reason: The study borrows the IOI task (after Wang et al.) as a testbed for distributed alignment search (DAS) on Pythia models. It aligns an ABAB-ABBA algorithm to the residual stream with identity, linear and non-linear maps, and reports interchange-intervention accuracy (IIA). It never identifies, ablates or patches attention heads, head classes or the GPT-2 small circuit. Its results concern how flexible DAS alignment maps are, not whether the IOI circuit holds. V5 concerns how faithful and complete the circuit looks; IIA of an algorithm alignment is a different construct, so no version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Correction: the distinct-name failure was for the randomly initialised model. The fully trained 410m model still aligned perfectly with non-linear maps and reasonably well with linear maps. The authors take this as showing generalisation should be part of causal-abstraction analysis. Their main conclusion is that unconstrained causal abstraction is vacuous: with expressive maps, any model can be aligned to any algorithm.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses distributed alignment search with identity, orthogonal linear, and reversible non-linear alignment maps, evaluating interchange-intervention accuracy against the ABAB-ABBA algorithm on Pythia models. It does not use the GPT-2 small head-ablation circuit-finding procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported IIA varies with alignment-map complexity, training checkpoint, and whether the training and evaluation sets share name entities.

fits_no_version.finding: Non-linear DAS maps reach perfect IOI ABAB-ABBA IIA on randomly initialised Pythia models (31M–410M) that cannot do the task.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: High IOI interchange-intervention accuracy from a flexible alignment map is not, by itself, evidence that a model implements the aligned algorithm.

fits_no_version.finding: IIA depends on alignment-map complexity: simpler non-linear maps reach perfect alignment only as training advances, and linear maps track the model's task accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Causal-abstraction results on IOI depend on the alignment-map family chosen.

fits_no_version.finding: With disjoint name sets, alignment fails for the random model but stays perfect (non-linear) or reasonably high (linear) for the trained model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Generalisation to held-out entities separates genuine algorithm alignment from memorisation by the alignment map.

record.problems: The text reports that one Pythia seed failed to learn IOI and another learned it but did not yield an alignment under the tested setup; the authors attribute the latter possibly to alignment-map training and note limited hyperparameter tuning. They also report that random-model alignment fails with disjoint name sets, indicating limited generalization. Numerical IIA values for these IOI conditions are presented in figures rather than stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No rows were added for the hierarchical equality or distributive-law tasks because they do not measure IOI. No separate rows were added for additional Pythia seeds in Figure 11: the text reports aggregate trends and exceptions but does not give numeric per-seed IOI values.

untested.parts: All of it: no GPT-2 small, no attention heads or head classes, no faithfulness, completeness or minimality tests.
All of it: no name-mover ablation and no backup-head analysis.
All of it: Pythia models and checkpoints are studied, but no head classes or roles are identified or compared.
All of it: no circuit is recovered by any method.
All of it: no circuit ablation, metric or prompt-distribution sensitivity of a circuit's faithfulness or completeness.
All of it: name-set splits vary the alignment map's train/test data, not the circuit across prompt formats.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V5 link conflates DAS alignment-map sensitivity with sensitivity of the IOI circuit's evaluation. The study never touches the GPT-2 small circuit or any head-level mechanism, so all rows are relinked to 'none' and no verdicts are given. The findings are kept under fits_no_version. Per-seed results (Fig. 11: one seed fails to learn IOI, another yields no alignment) are aggregate and also off-claim.

versions.untested_parts: GPT-2 small, the 26 attention heads and 7 classes, and the circuit’s faithfulness, completeness, and minimality criteria.
Ablating main name-mover heads and testing self-repair by backup heads.
Whether other models or checkpoints use the same head classes and roles, and whether circuit components are reused for other tasks.
Whether other circuit-finding methods, ablation types, or metrics recover the same GPT-2 small circuit.

The study varies alignment-map complexity and IOI name-set generalization, but does not test GPT-2 circuit ablations, the original circuit’s head-level roles, alternative circuit metrics, or how much behaviour lies outside that circuit.
Whether the same head mechanism carries IOI across name orders, templates, or prompts with more names.

relation.reason: Wang et al. is cited as inspiration for the IOI task. The study does not operationally use or test the circuit finding described by V1–V6.

tranche.reason: The study borrows the IOI task, but neither tests nor uses the claimed circuit finding. Its results concern algorithm alignment through DAS; no circuit head classes, backup mechanism or circuit evaluation is used.

source_check.notes: The main split excludes duplicate sentences but permits overlapping names. Appendix I.2.3 reports failure to align randomly initialized Pythia-410M with disjoint name sets and an alignment failure for one additional model seed.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Changing alignment-map complexity and training checkpoint in Pythia IOI experiments
reader_labels.reason: IIA changes with map complexity and training: the 8-layer non-linear map is near-perfect across checkpoints, the 4-layer map dips at step 1000, simpler non-linear maps reach perfect alignment later, and linear alignment only approximates it at full training (R7-R11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Pythia-410m with completely distinct training and evaluation name sets
reader_labels.reason: Name-set generalization changes the outcome: the randomly initialized model has no found alignment, while the fully trained model has perfect non-linear alignment and reasonably high linear alignment (R12-R14).
